weeks.assessment_key: CER rubric: 4 = Claim that the open system lost mass because CO₂ gas escaped; evidence with numbers (e.g., closed: 152.4 g before, 152.4 g after; open: 152.4 g → 150.1 g, a 2.3 g loss; bubbling observed); reasoning that atoms are rearranged, not destroyed (NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → NaCH₃COO + H₂O + CO₂), so mass is conserved in a closed system and the gas carried mass away in the open one. Balancing quiz key: 1) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. 2) 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. 3) C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 4) 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂. 5) N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. 6) 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂. 7) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. 8) 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. 9) Ca(OH)₂ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + 2H₂O. 10) C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O.

weeks.prep: Gather 3% hydrogen peroxide, active dry yeast, a tall glass or bottle, wooden splints or long matches, an iron nail (sanded clean), copper sulfate root killer (toxic — gloves, goggles, keep from children and pets, dispose per label) or vinegar + salt with dull pennies, Epsom salt (magnesium sulfate), washing soda (sodium carbonate — irritant, gloves), and clear cups. Print an activity series (K, Na, Ca, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, (H), Cu, Ag, Au).
misconceptions: Students think any metal can replace any other. A metal replaces another only if it is higher on the activity series.
Students think the precipitate is the original solid coming back. It is a new insoluble compound formed by swapping ion partners.
Students classify combustion and synthesis interchangeably. Combustion is a reaction with oxygen releasing energy (often a hydrocarbon making CO₂ and H₂O); synthesis is any A + B → AB.

days.guide: Pour ~50 mL of 3% peroxide into a tall glass and add a teaspoon of yeast. Light a splint, blow it out so it glows, and lower it into the foam (adult present). The student records observations and writes the balanced equation.

questions.q: Why does the glowing splint relight?
questions.a: The reaction produces oxygen gas, which makes the glowing wood burn faster.

questions.q: What role does the yeast play?
questions.a: It contains the enzyme catalase, a catalyst that speeds decomposition; it is not used up.

days.guide: With gloves and goggles, place a clean iron nail in copper sulfate solution (or soak pennies in vinegar + salt, then add a nail). Observe over 20 minutes and the next day. The student writes the equation and explains using the activity series.

questions.q: What is the reddish coating on the nail?
questions.a: Copper metal; iron replaced copper in solution because iron is more active.

questions.q: Why does the blue color fade?
questions.a: Blue Cu²⁺ ions are being removed from the solution and replaced by pale Fe²⁺ ions.

days.guide: Dissolve a spoon of Epsom salt in one cup of water and a spoon of washing soda in another, then mix. The student observes the precipitate, writes the equation, and identifies the swapped partners.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation and name the precipitate.
questions.a: MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃(s) + Na₂SO₄; the precipitate is magnesium carbonate.

questions.q: Why is this called double replacement?
questions.a: The cations and anions of two compounds swap partners.

days.guide: Model how to use the activity series. The student predicts whether 12 reactions occur and writes products for those that do.

questions.q: Will Al react with CuCl₂? If so, write the products.
questions.a: Yes; 2Al + 3CuCl₂ → 2AlCl₃ + 3Cu.

questions.q: Will Pb react with ZnCl₂?
questions.a: No — lead is below zinc.

days.guide: Give the quiz and grade together. Collect the lab notebook.

questions.q: Classify: 2KClO₃ → 2KCl + 3O₂
questions.a: Decomposition.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab notebook: full credit for observations, balanced equations and reaction types for all three labs: 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂ (decomposition; splint relights); Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (single replacement; copper coating, blue fades); MgSO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → MgCO₃(s) + Na₂SO₄ (double replacement; white precipitate). Quiz key: 1) 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO — synthesis. 2) CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — decomposition. 3) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ — single replacement. 4) AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃ — double replacement. 5) CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O — combustion. 6) Does Cu + ZnSO₄ react? No (Cu below Zn). 7) Does Zn + CuSO₄ react? Yes → ZnSO₄ + Cu. 8) Does Ag + HCl react? No (Ag below H). 9) Does Mg + 2HCl react? Yes → MgCl₂ + H₂. 10) Does Fe + 2AgNO₃ react? Yes → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag.

weeks.prep: Gather baking soda, vinegar, a cup, balloons, and the kitchen scale (0.01 g ideal). Formula card: NaHCO₃ = 84.01 g/mol; CO₂ = 44.01 g/mol; NaHCO₃ + CH₃COOH → NaCH₃COO + H₂O + CO₂.
misconceptions: Students convert grams of A directly to grams of B using the coefficients. Coefficients are mole ratios; always convert to moles first.
Students use the mole ratio upside down. Write the ratio with the unknown substance on top and the known on the bottom.
Students think percent yield over 100% is great. It signals an error (e.g., wet product or measurement error).

days.guide: Model reading mole ratios from coefficients. The student writes all ratios for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ and solves mole-to-mole problems.

questions.q: How many moles of NH₃ form from 6.0 mol H₂ (with enough N₂)?
questions.a: 6.0 mol H₂ × (2 mol NH₃ / 3 mol H₂) = 4.0 mol NH₃.

questions.q: In 2C₈H₁₈ + 25O₂ → 16CO₂ + 18H₂O, how many mol O₂ burn 1.0 mol octane?
questions.a: 12.5 mol O₂.

days.guide: Model the three-step road map: grams A → moles A → moles B → grams B. Work two examples, then assign eight problems.

questions.q: How many grams of water form when 16.0 g of CH₄ burns completely?
How many grams of NH₃ form from 28.0 g of N₂?

days.guide: The student predicts the mass of CO₂ from 5.0 g baking soda, then weighs a cup of excess vinegar plus the baking soda on paper, adds the baking soda slowly, waits until bubbling stops, swirls, and reweighs everything (including the paper). Mass lost = CO₂ released.

questions.q: Predict the mass of CO₂ produced from 5.0 g of NaHCO₃.
Why add the baking soda slowly?
questions.a: To avoid foam overflowing, which would lose liquid mass and make the CO₂ loss appear too large.

days.guide: The student calculates percent yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100 and analyzes errors.

questions.q: You measured 2.1 g of CO₂ lost; the theoretical value is 2.6 g. What is the percent yield?
Why might the measured CO₂ be low?
questions.a: Some CO₂ stays dissolved in the liquid; also the reaction may not be complete or readings may be imprecise.

days.guide: Give the stoichiometry quiz with a periodic table. Grade together and redo missed problems.

questions.q: How many grams of O₂ are needed to burn 16.0 g of CH₄?

weeks.assessment_key: Lab: full credit for predicted CO₂ (5.0 g ÷ 84.01 = 0.0595 mol → 0.0595 × 44.01 = 2.6 g), measured mass loss, percent yield, and two error sources (CO₂ staying dissolved in the liquid, splashing, water evaporating, incomplete reaction). Quiz key: 1) In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, mol H₂O from 4.0 mol O₂ — 8.0 mol. 2) In N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃, mol H₂ needed for 5.0 mol N₂ — 15 mol. 3) Grams NH₃ from 28.0 g N₂ — 34.1 g. 4) Grams H₂O from 16.0 g CH₄ burned — 35.9 g. 5) Grams O₂ needed to burn 16.0 g CH₄ — 63.9 g (≈ 64 g). 6) Theoretical yield 2.6 g, actual 2.1 g — 81% (80.8%). 7) Grams CO₂ from 10.0 g C₃H₈ (C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O): 10.0 ÷ 44.09 = 0.227 mol × 3 × 44.01 = 29.9 g.

weeks.prep: Gather bread and cheese slices (or cards labeled as such), baking soda, vinegar (5% acetic acid), five identical bottles and balloons, a measuring spoon or scale, and a flexible measuring tape. Open PhET 'Reactants, Products and Leftovers'.
misconceptions: Students assume the reactant with the smaller mass is limiting. Compare moles needed vs. moles available using the balanced ratio.
Students think that once one reactant is used up the other keeps reacting. The reaction stops when the limiting reactant is gone; the excess remains.
Students calculate product from both reactants and add them. The smaller amount of product is the correct (theoretical) yield.

days.guide: Model making sandwiches (2 bread + 1 cheese). Give different quantities and have the student find how many sandwiches can be made, what runs out, and what is left over.

questions.q: You have 12 slices of bread and 4 slices of cheese. How many sandwiches, and what is limiting?
questions.a: 4 sandwiches; cheese is limiting; 4 slices of bread are left.

questions.q: Relate this to a chemical reaction.
questions.a: The balanced equation is the recipe; the reactant that runs out first limits how much product forms.

days.guide: In PhET, the student completes the sandwich and molecule screens, predicting products and leftovers before checking. Record three cases.

questions.q: With 4 N₂ and 9 H₂ molecules (N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃), what forms and what is left?
questions.a: H₂ limits: 9 H₂ make 6 NH₃ using 3 N₂; 1 N₂ is left over.

questions.q: With 3 CH₄ and 4 O₂ (CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O), what forms?
questions.a: O₂ limits: 2 CH₄ react making 2 CO₂ and 4 H₂O; 1 CH₄ left over.

days.guide: Put 100 mL of vinegar in each of five bottles. Put 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 g of baking soda into balloons, stretch each over a bottle, then lift to dump. After reactions stop, measure balloon circumference and graph.

questions.q: Why do the last balloons end up about the same size?
questions.a: The vinegar ran out (became limiting), so extra baking soda could not make more CO₂.

questions.q: Estimate the baking soda mass at which 100 mL of 5% vinegar becomes limiting.
questions.a: ≈ 5 g acetic acid ÷ 60.05 = 0.083 mol → 0.083 × 84.01 ≈ 7 g baking soda.

days.guide: Model a limiting reactant problem for methane combustion; the student solves four more for fuels.

questions.q: 10.0 g CH₄ reacts with 32.0 g O₂. Which is limiting and how much CO₂ forms?
questions.a: CH₄: 0.623 mol needs 1.25 mol O₂, but only 1.00 mol O₂ is available → O₂ limits. CO₂ = 1.00 ÷ 2 = 0.500 mol × 44.01 = 22.0 g.

questions.q: In a car engine with too little air, what forms instead of CO₂, and why is it dangerous?
questions.a: Carbon monoxide (CO) and soot from incomplete combustion; CO binds to hemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Grade together and collect the balloon graph.

questions.q: 4.0 mol Al reacts with 4.0 mol Cl₂ (2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃). Which is limiting and how much AlCl₃ forms?
questions.a: Cl₂ limits (4.0 mol Al needs 6.0 mol Cl₂); AlCl₃ = 4.0 × 2/3 = 2.7 mol.

weeks.assessment_key: Balloon lab: full credit for a graph of baking soda mass (x) vs. balloon circumference (y) that rises and then levels off; identification of the leveling point. With 100 mL vinegar (≈0.083 mol acetic acid), growth should stop near 7 g baking soda (0.083 × 84.01). Explanation: before that point baking soda is limiting; after it vinegar is limiting. Quiz key: 1) 10 slices of bread and 8 cheese, sandwich = 2 bread + 1 cheese: 5 sandwiches, bread limiting, 3 cheese left. 2) 10.0 g CH₄ + 32.0 g O₂: O₂ limiting (needs 1.25 mol O₂, has 1.00 mol); CO₂ = 0.500 mol = 22.0 g; leftover CH₄ = 1.98 g. 3) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O with 4.0 mol H₂ and 3.0 mol O₂: H₂ limiting; 4.0 mol H₂O; 1.0 mol O₂ left. 4) N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ with 2.0 mol N₂ and 3.0 mol H₂: H₂ limiting; 2.0 mol NH₃.

weeks.prep: Gather baking soda, vinegar, 3% hydrogen peroxide, yeast, two cups, and a thermometer. Prepare a bond-energy table (kJ/mol): C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O (in CO₂) 799, O–H 463, H–H 436, N≡N 945, N–H 391. Build the Unit 5 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think breaking bonds releases energy (like breaking a stick). Breaking bonds always requires energy; forming bonds releases energy.
Students reverse the sign: ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed; a negative ΔH is exothermic.
Students think exothermic reactions need no activation energy. Even exothermic reactions (like burning wood) need an initial energy input to start.

days.guide: Mix baking soda and vinegar in a cup with a thermometer and record the temperature change; then mix yeast into peroxide and record. The student classifies each as endo- or exothermic.

questions.q: The baking soda reaction dropped from 21 °C to 17 °C. Endothermic or exothermic?
questions.a: Endothermic — it absorbed energy from the surroundings.

questions.q: The peroxide reaction rose from 21 °C to 35 °C. What does that tell you about bonds?
questions.a: Exothermic — more energy was released forming bonds in H₂O and O₂ than was absorbed breaking bonds in H₂O₂.

days.guide: Model an energy diagram: reactant level, hump (activation energy), product level, and ΔH arrow. The student draws one for each Day 1 reaction and labels them.

questions.q: On an exothermic energy diagram, are products higher or lower than reactants?
questions.a: Lower — energy is released.

questions.q: What does a catalyst do to the diagram?
questions.a: It lowers the activation energy hump; ΔH is unchanged.

days.guide: Model ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) for methane combustion step by step. The student then does H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl and 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.q: Calculate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
Calculate ΔH for 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

days.guide: Use two magnets as a model: pulling them apart takes energy (breaking), letting them snap together releases energy (forming). The student builds a written or physical model explaining why combustion is exothermic overall.

questions.q: Why is burning methane exothermic overall if breaking its bonds absorbs energy?
questions.a: The bonds formed in CO₂ and H₂O are stronger in total, releasing more energy (3450 kJ) than was absorbed breaking the reactant bonds (2648 kJ).

questions.q: What does the magnet model represent?
questions.a: Atoms attracting; separating them requires energy input and bringing them together releases energy.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test (50 minutes) with periodic table, bond-energy table and activity series. Grade together.

questions.q: Is photosynthesis endothermic or exothermic?
questions.a: Endothermic — it absorbs light energy to make glucose.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 5 test key (sample): 1) Balance Fe₂O₃ + CO → Fe + CO₂: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. 2) Classify AgNO₃ + KCl → AgCl + KNO₃: double replacement. 3) Grams CO₂ from 12.0 g C burned (C + O₂ → CO₂): 44.0 g. 4) 5.0 mol H₂ and 2.0 mol O₂ (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O): O₂ limits, 4.0 mol H₂O. 5) Percent yield, 18.0 g theoretical, 15.3 g actual: 85.0%. 6) ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O from bond energies: −802 kJ/mol. 7) ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431): (436 + 242) − 2(431) = −184 kJ (exothermic). 8) Endothermic or exothermic: baking soda + vinegar — endothermic (temperature drops). 9) Label an energy diagram: reactants, products, activation energy, ΔH. 10) Explain why forming bonds releases energy — atoms reach a lower, more stable energy state.

weeks.prep: Gather two identical jars, plastic wrap, a rubber band, two thermometers, a lamp with an incandescent or halogen bulb (or sunlight), and black and white paper. Bookmark NASA's Earth energy budget diagram and PhET 'Greenhouse Effect'. Make a data table.
misconceptions: Students think the greenhouse effect is the ozone hole. They are different problems; ozone depletion lets in more UV, while greenhouse gases absorb outgoing infrared.
Students think greenhouse gases trap sunlight coming in. Most incoming sunlight is visible light that passes through; greenhouse gases absorb the infrared Earth emits.
Students think the greenhouse effect is entirely bad. Without it Earth's average temperature would be about −18 °C instead of about +15 °C; the problem is the enhanced effect from added gases.

days.guide: Using NASA's diagram, the student draws Earth's energy budget: incoming sunlight (~340 W/m² average), ~30% reflected by clouds, air and surface, ~70% absorbed, and outgoing infrared, with the atmosphere re-radiating some back down. Discuss what 'balance' means.

questions.q: What happens to Earth's temperature if more energy comes in than goes out?
questions.a: Earth warms until outgoing infrared increases enough to restore balance.

questions.q: About what fraction of incoming sunlight is reflected?
questions.a: About 30%.

days.guide: Wrap one thermometer bulb in black paper and one in white; place both in sun for 15 minutes, reading every 3 minutes. The student graphs and explains in terms of albedo.

questions.q: Which warmed more and why?
questions.a: Black paper — it has low albedo, absorbing more light and converting it to thermal energy.

questions.q: Why does Arctic sea ice loss speed up warming?
questions.a: Dark ocean replaces reflective ice, lowering albedo so more sunlight is absorbed.

days.guide: Place thermometers in two jars under a lamp; cover one with plastic wrap. Record temperatures every 5 minutes for 30 minutes and graph. Discuss honestly what the model does and does not show.

questions.q: Why did the covered jar get warmer?
questions.a: Mostly because the cover traps warm air (stops convection and mixing with room air); it is a model of energy trapping but not the same mechanism as CO₂ absorbing infrared.

questions.q: How could you better model the real greenhouse effect?
questions.a: Compare two covered jars, one filled with extra CO₂ (from baking soda and vinegar), keeping everything else the same.

days.guide: In PhET Greenhouse Effect (photon absorption screen), the student shines infrared on N₂, O₂, CO₂, H₂O and CH₄ and records which absorb it and how they move. Explain using bond vibrations that change the molecule's charge distribution.

questions.q: Why does CO₂ absorb infrared but N₂ does not?
questions.a: CO₂ can bend and stretch in ways that create a temporary dipole, letting it absorb IR; N₂ is a symmetric diatomic whose vibration produces no dipole change.

questions.q: After a CO₂ molecule absorbs infrared, what happens to the energy?
questions.a: It is re-emitted in a random direction (some back toward Earth) or transferred to nearby molecules by collisions, warming the air.

days.guide: Give the energy-balance quiz and grade together. Collect lab data.

questions.q: Why is water vapor considered a feedback rather than a driver of climate change?
questions.a: Its amount depends on temperature: warmer air holds more water vapor, which amplifies warming started by other gases like CO₂.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab data: full credit for temperature tables every 5 minutes, graphs of both trials, and correct conclusions (black paper warmed more than white; covered jar warmed more than open). The write-up should note honestly that a sealed jar warms mainly because it blocks convection, which is different from how CO₂ works in the atmosphere. Quiz key: 1) Earth reflects about 30% of incoming sunlight (albedo ≈ 0.3). 2) Earth emits energy as infrared radiation. 3) Greenhouse gases include CO₂, H₂O, CH₄, N₂O. 4) Why N₂ and O₂ don't absorb IR — symmetric two-atom molecules; vibrating doesn't change their dipole. 5) Without greenhouse gases Earth would average about −18 °C. 6) Melting ice lowers albedo, so more sunlight is absorbed. 7) If incoming energy exceeds outgoing, Earth warms until balance returns. 8) Black surfaces have low albedo and absorb more.

weeks.prep: Print a NOAA or NASA carbon-cycle diagram with reservoirs (GtC) and fluxes (GtC/yr). Gather chalk or limestone (or seashells), vinegar, a calculator and a spreadsheet. Approximate values to use: atmosphere ~875 GtC (pre-2020 diagrams; about 900 today), surface ocean ~900, deep ocean ~37,000, vegetation ~450–650, soils ~1,500–2,400, fossil fuel reserves ~1,000+, sedimentary rocks ~60–100 million GtC; human emissions ~10 GtC/yr; 1 ppm CO₂ ≈ 2.13 GtC.
misconceptions: Students think carbon is 'used up' in the cycle. Carbon atoms are conserved; they move among reservoirs.
Students think all human CO₂ stays in the air. About half is absorbed by oceans and land; roughly 45% remains in the atmosphere.
Students confuse reservoirs (amounts, GtC) with fluxes (rates, GtC/yr). Use units to tell them apart.

days.guide: Using the diagram, the student makes a table of reservoirs (GtC) and fluxes (GtC/yr): photosynthesis, respiration/decay, ocean uptake/release, volcanism, fossil fuel burning. Ask which reservoir is largest and which flux humans added.

questions.q: Which reservoir holds the most carbon?
questions.a: Sedimentary rocks (limestone and organic carbon) — tens of millions of GtC; among the fast-cycle reservoirs, the deep ocean (~37,000 GtC).

questions.q: What process moves carbon from the atmosphere to the biosphere?
questions.a: Photosynthesis (6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂).

days.guide: Build a spreadsheet box model: Year, Atmospheric carbon, Natural in, Natural out (equal). Start with natural fluxes balanced so the line stays flat. The student explains why a balanced system is steady.

questions.q: If natural inflows equal outflows, what happens to atmospheric carbon over time?
questions.a: It stays constant (steady state).

questions.q: Convert 875 GtC of atmospheric carbon to ppm of CO₂.

days.guide: Add human emissions (10 GtC/yr) with 55% taken up by sinks. The student graphs 50 years, converts to ppm, and compares the slope to the Keeling Curve's recent ~2.4 ppm/yr.

questions.q: With 10 GtC/yr emitted and 45% remaining, how fast does atmospheric CO₂ rise in ppm/yr?
questions.a: 4.5 GtC/yr ÷ 2.13 ≈ 2.1 ppm/yr.

questions.q: Why might the model underestimate the real rise?
questions.a: Emissions are growing rather than constant, and sinks may absorb a smaller fraction over time.

days.guide: Drop vinegar on chalk or limestone and observe fizzing. Write the reaction and connect to carbon stored in rocks and the slow carbon cycle (weathering, burial, volcanic release).

questions.q: Write the equation for vinegar reacting with limestone.
questions.a: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂

questions.q: How did carbon get into limestone originally?
questions.a: Marine organisms built shells from dissolved calcium and carbonate; the shells accumulated and became rock.

days.guide: The student writes a model explanation with the spreadsheet graph, explaining reservoirs, fluxes, human perturbation and limitations. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: Why is burning fossil fuels a problem for the carbon cycle if the carbon was originally in the atmosphere?
questions.a: It moves carbon stored over millions of years in the slow cycle into the atmosphere in decades, much faster than natural processes can remove it.

weeks.assessment_key: Model rubric (4 levels): 4 = Spreadsheet with year column, atmospheric carbon (starting ~875 GtC), natural fluxes in and out balanced, human emissions (~10 GtC/yr) with about 55% absorbed by sinks, conversion to ppm (÷ 2.13), and a graph over 50 years showing ~2.1 ppm/yr increase (close to the observed ~2.4 ppm/yr); written explanation of assumptions, comparison to Keeling Curve data, and one limitation (e.g., constant emissions or constant sink fraction). 3 = working model but weak comparison. 2 = model errors (mixing reservoirs and fluxes). 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Download NOAA Mauna Loa annual mean CO₂ (gml.noaa.gov/ccgg/trends) and Vostok ice core CO₂ and temperature data (NOAA Paleoclimatology or CDIAC). Open NASA Climate 'Vital Signs' and Cal-Adapt (cal-adapt.org) for California projections. Prepare a spreadsheet.
misconceptions: Students think correlation in ice cores proves CO₂ alone drove past cycles. In ice ages, orbital changes started warming and CO₂ then amplified it (a feedback); today CO₂ is rising first because of human emissions.
Students think the yearly Keeling sawtooth is pollution changing seasonally. It is Northern Hemisphere plants taking up CO₂ in summer and releasing it in winter.
Students think 'positive feedback' means good. Positive feedback amplifies a change; negative feedback dampens it.

days.guide: The student graphs Mauna Loa annual mean CO₂ from 1959 to the latest year, calculates the average yearly increase overall and for the last ten years, and describes the shape (accelerating). Discuss the monthly sawtooth.

questions.q: CO₂ was about 317 ppm in 1960 and 425 ppm in 2024. What is the average annual increase?
Why does CO₂ drop each Northern Hemisphere summer?
questions.a: Plants in the Northern Hemisphere, which has most of the land, absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis during the growing season.

days.guide: Graph Vostok CO₂ and temperature on the same time axis (or a scatter plot). The student describes the correlation and compares the maximum ice-core value with today.

questions.q: What relationship do the Vostok data show?
questions.a: A strong positive correlation: warm interglacials have high CO₂ (~280–300 ppm) and ice ages have low CO₂ (~180 ppm).

questions.q: How do the bubbles in ice record past CO₂?
questions.a: Air trapped in the ice as snow compacts preserves samples of the ancient atmosphere.

days.guide: The student draws loop diagrams for the ice-albedo and permafrost feedbacks, with + signs on each arrow, and one negative feedback for contrast (e.g., warmer Earth radiates more infrared).

questions.q: Explain the permafrost feedback.
questions.a: Warming thaws frozen soil; microbes decompose organic matter, releasing CO₂ and methane, which cause more warming.

questions.q: Give an example of a negative feedback.
questions.a: A warmer Earth emits more infrared radiation to space, which tends to cool it.

days.guide: Use Cal-Adapt or NASA projections to compare a lower-emissions and higher-emissions scenario for the student's region in 2050 (temperature, extreme-heat days, Sierra snowpack). The student writes a short forecast with numbers and sources.

questions.q: Why do forecasts give two or more scenarios?
questions.a: Future warming depends on how much greenhouse gas humans emit, which is uncertain; scenarios show outcomes for different emission paths.

questions.q: Why does Sierra snowpack matter to California?
questions.a: It stores water that melts in spring and summer, supplying a large share of the state's water; less snowpack means less stored water when it's needed.

days.guide: Give the data-analysis quiz (graph reading and calculations). Grade together.

questions.q: A graph shows global temperature rising 0.2 °C per decade. How much warming is that over 30 years?

weeks.assessment_key: Forecast write-up rubric: 4 = Uses NASA/Cal-Adapt projections to state a 2050 California temperature change under lower and higher emissions (roughly +2 to +4 °F above late-20th-century averages, larger under high emissions) and the direction of snowpack change (substantial decline, larger under high emissions), cites the data source and explains uncertainty and the role of feedbacks. Quiz key: 1) Mauna Loa CO₂ rose from about 317 ppm (1960) to about 425 ppm (2024): average ≈ 1.7 ppm/yr; recent decade ≈ 2.4–2.5 ppm/yr. 2) Vostok CO₂ ranged ~180–300 ppm over 400,000 years. 3) Today's ~425 ppm is far above any value in the 800,000-year ice-core record. 4) Ice-albedo feedback: warming melts ice → lower albedo → more absorption → more warming (positive). 5) Permafrost feedback: thawing releases CO₂ and CH₄ → more warming (positive). 6) The seasonal cycle is caused by Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis/respiration.

weeks.prep: Gather research sources: NREL or Department of Energy pages on solar and EVs, IEA or DOE pages on carbon capture, California Air Resources Board pages on cap-and-trade (renamed cap-and-invest when extended in 2025) and SB 32. Build the Unit 6 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think EVs produce zero emissions under all conditions. Their emissions depend on how electricity is generated and on battery manufacturing, though lifetime emissions are generally lower than gasoline cars.
Students think one solution will solve climate change. Use the trade-off matrix to show that combinations are needed.
Students confuse SB 32 targets with AB 32. AB 32 (2006): return to 1990 levels by 2020. SB 32 (2016): 40% below 1990 levels by 2030.

days.guide: The student researches solar PV, EVs and carbon capture, filling a table: how it works chemically, CO₂ reduced, cost, limitations. Check that chemistry is explained (e.g., electrons freed in silicon by light).

questions.q: How does a solar cell produce electricity?
questions.a: Photons give energy to electrons in a silicon semiconductor; an internal electric field at the p-n junction pushes them through a circuit.

questions.q: How does a common carbon-capture method trap CO₂?
questions.a: Flue gas passes through an amine solution that chemically binds CO₂; heating later releases pure CO₂ for storage underground.

days.guide: Build a decision matrix: rows = solutions, columns = criteria (cost, CO₂ reduction, feasibility, time to deploy), weighted by importance. The student scores each and totals.

questions.q: Why weight criteria differently?
questions.a: Some criteria matter more to the decision-maker (e.g., CO₂ reduction may count double), so weights reflect priorities.

questions.q: What is a trade-off?
questions.a: Giving up some of one desirable quality to gain another (e.g., higher cost for greater CO₂ reduction).

days.guide: Read about California's cap-and-trade program (started 2013, extended in 2025 as cap-and-invest) and the SB 32 goal. The student summarizes how a cap works and lists one argument for and one against.

questions.q: What does SB 32 require?
questions.a: That California cut greenhouse gas emissions to 40% below 1990 levels by 2030.

questions.q: How does cap-and-trade reduce emissions?
questions.a: The state sets a declining cap on total emissions and issues allowances; companies that cut emissions cheaply can sell spare allowances, so reductions happen where cheapest.

days.guide: The student writes a 1-page brief recommending one solution for the city, with evidence and trade-offs. Score with the rubric; revise once.

questions.q: What should the brief's recommendation sentence include?
questions.a: The specific action, who should do it, and the main benefit (e.g., 'The city should install solar panels on all public buildings by 2030 to cut X tons of CO₂ per year').

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Grade together.

questions.q: What is the chemistry behind an EV battery's charge and discharge?
questions.a: Lithium ions move from the anode to the cathode through the electrolyte while electrons flow through the circuit (discharge); charging reverses the flow.

weeks.assessment_key: Position brief rubric: 4 = Clear recommendation for the student's city; explains the chemistry (e.g., photovoltaic silicon converting light to electricity; lithium-ion batteries moving Li⁺ ions; amines binding CO₂); uses data (cost, tons of CO₂ avoided); acknowledges trade-offs; cites ≥3 sources. Unit 6 test key (sample): 1) Albedo of Earth ≈ 0.3. 2) Why CO₂ absorbs IR — vibrations change its dipole. 3) 1 ppm CO₂ ≈ 2.13 GtC; adding 4.26 GtC raises CO₂ by 2 ppm. 4) Largest active reservoir — deep ocean. 5) Ice-albedo feedback is positive. 6) SB 32 target — 40% below 1990 by 2030. 7) Cap-and-trade sets a declining limit on total emissions and lets companies buy/sell allowances. 8) One trade-off of carbon capture — high energy cost and expense. 9) The Keeling Curve's seasonal cycle comes from Northern Hemisphere photosynthesis. 10) Mitigation vs. adaptation: mitigation reduces emissions; adaptation copes with impacts.

weeks.prep: Gather Alka-Seltzer tablets (6+), clear cups, ice water, room-temperature water and hot tap water (~45–50 °C), a thermometer, a stopwatch, a spoon or mortar for crushing, 3% hydrogen peroxide and yeast. Open PhET 'Reactions & Rates'.
misconceptions: Students think a catalyst is consumed. It speeds the reaction by providing a lower-activation-energy pathway and is recovered unchanged.
Students say heat makes particles collide only more often. Higher temperature also makes a larger fraction of collisions energetic enough to exceed the activation energy — the bigger effect.
Students think crushing a tablet changes how much gas forms. It changes the rate, not the total amount of product.

days.guide: In PhET Reactions & Rates, the student runs single collisions with low and high energy, then many-molecule runs at different temperatures, recording how often reactions happen. Introduce the four factors (temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst).

questions.q: According to collision theory, what two conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
questions.a: Enough energy (at least the activation energy) and the correct orientation.

questions.q: Why does increasing concentration speed a reaction?
questions.a: More particles per volume means more frequent collisions.

days.guide: Put equal volumes of ice water, room-temperature water and hot water in three cups, record temperatures, and time a whole tablet dissolving in each. Repeat once. The student graphs temperature vs. time.

questions.q: Predict the effect of raising the temperature by 10 °C.
questions.a: The reaction speeds up — for many reactions roughly doubling the rate.

questions.q: Explain the result with collision theory.
questions.a: Particles in hot water move faster, colliding more often and with more energy, so more collisions exceed the activation energy.

days.guide: Time a whole tablet and a crushed tablet (same mass) in equal room-temperature water. The student explains the difference and connects to real examples (flour-dust explosions, kindling vs. logs).

questions.q: Which dissolved faster and why?
questions.a: The crushed tablet — more surface area exposes more particles to collisions with water.

questions.q: Why do grain silos risk dust explosions?
questions.a: Fine dust has an enormous surface area, so it can burn extremely rapidly when ignited.

days.guide: Pour peroxide into two cups; add yeast to one only. Compare bubbling. The student draws an energy diagram showing the catalyzed and uncatalyzed paths.

questions.q: How does catalase speed the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide?
questions.a: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed.

questions.q: Is the yeast used up?
questions.a: No — the enzyme is a catalyst; it is not consumed (though it can eventually denature).

days.guide: The student writes the rate lab report. Score with the rubric and have the student revise the explanation section.

questions.q: Why do we refrigerate food?
questions.a: Lower temperature slows the chemical reactions and bacterial growth that spoil food.

weeks.assessment_key: Lab report rubric: 4 = Question, hypothesis, controlled variables (same water volume, tablet size), data table with times for cold/room/hot and whole/crushed (with trials), graph of temperature vs. dissolving time showing time decreases as temperature rises; explanation using collision theory (faster particles → more frequent collisions and more collisions with energy ≥ activation energy; crushing increases surface area so more particles are exposed; yeast's catalase lowers activation energy); error analysis and improvement. 3 = correct data and partial collision-theory explanation. 2 = data with little explanation. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather two identical clear cups, water, two straws of different diameters, a measuring cup or ruler, and graph paper. Open a sealed bottle of soda for Day 4 discussion.
misconceptions: Students think at equilibrium the amounts of reactants and products are equal. At equilibrium the forward and reverse rates are equal; concentrations are constant but usually not equal.
Students think reactions stop at equilibrium. Both reactions continue (dynamic); there is no net change.
Students include solids and pure liquids in K expressions. Only gases and dissolved species appear.

days.guide: Introduce reversible reactions with examples (N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂, water evaporating and condensing in a closed bottle). The student defines dynamic equilibrium and sketches a concentration vs. time graph showing curves leveling off.

questions.q: In a sealed water bottle, why does the water level stop dropping?
questions.a: The evaporation rate becomes equal to the condensation rate.

questions.q: What does the double arrow ⇌ mean?
questions.a: The reaction is reversible; it proceeds in both directions.

days.guide: Fill cup A with 200 mL water and leave cup B empty. Each 'turn,' the student uses the wide straw to move water A → B and the partner (or student, second hand) uses the narrow straw B → A simultaneously by pinching the straw top. Record levels every turn for 20 turns and graph.

questions.q: Why did the levels stop changing even though water kept moving?
questions.a: The amount moved A → B each turn equaled the amount moved B → A — equal forward and reverse rates.

questions.q: Were the final volumes equal? Why or why not?
questions.a: No; the different straw sizes mean equal transfer happens only when the cup with the narrow straw is much fuller.

days.guide: Teach K = [products]^coefficients ÷ [reactants]^coefficients. The student writes K for five reactions and interprets large and small values.

questions.q: Write K for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.
questions.a: K = [SO₃]² ÷ ([SO₂]²[O₂])

questions.q: If K = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰, which side is favored?
questions.a: Reactants — very little product at equilibrium.

days.guide: Discuss a sealed soda: CO₂(g) above the liquid ⇌ CO₂(aq), and CO₂(aq) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃. Open the bottle and observe. The student explains what changes when the cap comes off.

questions.q: Why doesn't a sealed soda keep bubbling?
questions.a: The CO₂ in the gas space and dissolved CO₂ are at equilibrium; escape and dissolving rates are equal.

questions.q: Why does it fizz when opened?
questions.a: Pressure of CO₂ above the liquid drops, so CO₂ comes out of solution faster than it dissolves until a new equilibrium (mostly flat soda) is reached.

days.guide: Give the equilibrium quiz and grade together.

questions.q: Write K for CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g).
questions.a: K = [CO₂] (solids are left out).

weeks.assessment_key: Model graph: full credit for water level vs. transfer number for both cups, curves that level off at unequal heights, and the explanation that equilibrium was reached when the amount moved each way per turn became equal. Quiz key: 1) Define dynamic equilibrium — forward and reverse rates equal; concentrations constant. 2) K for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: K = [NH₃]² ÷ ([N₂][H₂]³). 3) K for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: [HI]² ÷ ([H₂][I₂]). 4) K = 1 × 10⁸ means products are strongly favored. 5) K = 1 × 10⁻⁵ means reactants favored. 6) In a sealed soda, CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) at equilibrium. 7) Why the water levels weren't equal — different straw sizes make different transfer rates; equilibrium is about equal rates. 8) Is equilibrium static? No — dynamic.

weeks.prep: Make red cabbage indicator: chop 2 cups of red cabbage, cover with boiling water, steep 15 minutes, strain and refrigerate. Gather vinegar, baking soda, clear cups, two sodas (one cold, one warm), and ice/warm water baths. Print a description of the Haber process.
misconceptions: Students think Le Chatelier means the system returns to its original state. It shifts to partially counteract the stress and settles at a new equilibrium.
Students think adding a catalyst shifts equilibrium. A catalyst speeds both directions equally; it gets to equilibrium faster without changing the yield.
Students treat temperature like concentration without considering ΔH. For an exothermic reaction, heat is a 'product', so raising temperature shifts left.

days.guide: Teach Le Chatelier's principle with stresses: add/remove reactant or product, change temperature, change pressure. The student predicts shifts for 10 cases using N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat and explains each.

questions.q: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ + heat, what happens if the temperature is raised?
questions.a: The equilibrium shifts left (toward N₂ and H₂), absorbing the added heat; less NH₃.

questions.q: What happens if N₂ is added?
questions.a: Shifts right, using up some added N₂ and producing more NH₃.

days.guide: Put cabbage indicator in three cups: add vinegar to one and baking-soda solution to another; keep one neutral. Then add base to the acid cup drop by drop and watch the color shift back. Explain that indicator molecules exist in an equilibrium between acid and base forms.

questions.q: What color is cabbage indicator in vinegar and in baking-soda solution?
questions.a: Pink/red in vinegar (acid); blue-green in baking-soda solution (base); purple near neutral.

questions.q: Why does adding base to the pink cup change its color?
questions.a: Base removes H⁺ ions, shifting the indicator's equilibrium toward its base-colored form.

days.guide: Open a cold soda and a warm soda (in a sink!) and compare fizz. The student explains with equilibrium: CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) + heat.

questions.q: Which soda fizzed more and why?
questions.a: The warm soda; gas solubility decreases at higher temperature, so the equilibrium shifts toward gaseous CO₂.

questions.q: Why does warm lake water hold less oxygen for fish?
questions.a: Gases are less soluble in warmer water, so less O₂ stays dissolved.

days.guide: Present the Haber process and real conditions (~200 atm, ~400–450 °C, iron catalyst, NH₃ removed by cooling). The student proposes conditions to maximize yield and explains the trade-offs.

questions.q: Why not run the Haber process at room temperature if low temperature favors ammonia?
questions.a: The reaction would be far too slow; a moderate temperature with a catalyst gives an acceptable rate with a reasonable yield.

questions.q: Why does high pressure increase the yield?
questions.a: The product side has fewer gas molecules (2 vs. 4), so increasing pressure shifts toward ammonia.

days.guide: Give the Le Chatelier quiz and collect the design proposal.

questions.q: For CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g), which way does decreasing pressure shift it?
questions.a: Left, toward the side with more gas molecules (4 vs. 2).

weeks.assessment_key: Design proposal rubric: 4 = For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = −92 kJ): high pressure (shifts toward fewer gas moles, 2 vs. 4); removing NH₃ by condensing it; adding excess N₂/H₂; a compromise moderate temperature (~400–450 °C) because low temperature favors yield but is too slow; iron catalyst for rate; trade-offs of cost and safety of high pressure. Quiz key: 1) Adding H₂ shifts right. 2) Removing NH₃ shifts right. 3) Raising temperature of an exothermic reaction shifts left. 4) Increasing pressure for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts right. 5) Increasing pressure for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI: no shift (2 gas moles each side). 6) Catalyst: no shift. 7) Cold soda holds more CO₂ because CO₂ dissolving is exothermic / gas solubility is higher at low temperature. 8) Adding acid to cabbage indicator turns it pink-red (shifts the indicator's equilibrium to its acid form).

weeks.prep: Print overviews of the Contact process for sulfuric acid (2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃, ΔH ≈ −198 kJ, vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, ~400–450 °C, near 1–2 atm with excess air) or methanol synthesis (CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, ΔH ≈ −91 kJ, copper/zinc oxide catalyst, ~250 °C, 50–100 atm). Build the Unit 7 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students choose the highest-yield conditions regardless of cost or speed. Industrial chemists optimize rate, yield, cost and safety together.
Students think pressure always helps. Pressure only shifts equilibria involving unequal moles of gas, and high pressure is expensive and hazardous.
Students forget that recycling unreacted gases is a key way to improve overall yield.

days.guide: The student reads the case study and summarizes the equation, ΔH, catalyst, conditions and uses (sulfuric acid: fertilizers, batteries; methanol: fuels, plastics).

questions.q: For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic), why is a catalyst used?
questions.a: To speed the reaction at a moderate temperature where yield is still good.

questions.q: What is sulfuric acid mostly used for?
questions.a: Making phosphate fertilizers (also batteries and chemical processing).

days.guide: The student proposes changes to temperature, pressure, concentrations and catalyst and explains each effect on rate and yield in a table, plus trade-offs.

questions.q: For methanol synthesis (CO + 2H₂ ⇌ CH₃OH, exothermic), what pressure change improves yield?
questions.a: Higher pressure — 3 gas moles become 1.

questions.q: What is a trade-off of very high pressure?
questions.a: Stronger, costlier equipment and greater safety risk.

days.guide: The student presents the design to you; ask probing questions (Why that temperature? What happens to unreacted gas? Is it safe?). The student records questions he or she could not answer.

questions.q: How can a plant increase overall yield without changing equilibrium?
questions.a: Separate the product and recycle the unreacted reactants back through the reactor.

questions.q: Does the catalyst change the equilibrium yield?
questions.a: No, only how fast equilibrium is reached.

days.guide: The student revises the proposal to address feedback, marking changes.

questions.q: Why might an engineer accept a lower yield per pass?
questions.a: Higher temperature gives a much faster rate, so more product is made per hour overall, especially with recycling.

days.guide: Give the Unit 7 test. Grade together.

questions.q: For H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), does increasing pressure change the yield?
questions.a: No — there are 2 moles of gas on each side.

weeks.assessment_key: Design proposal rubric: 4 = Correct equation and ΔH; predicted effect of temperature, pressure, concentration and catalyst on both rate and yield; chosen operating conditions with justification; at least two trade-offs (cost, safety, energy, rate); revision based on feedback. Unit 7 test key (sample): 1) Four factors affecting rate: temperature, concentration, surface area, catalyst. 2) Why temperature speeds reactions — more frequent, more energetic collisions; more exceed Ea. 3) Catalyst lowers activation energy; does not change K or yield. 4) K for 2NO₂ ⇌ N₂O₄: [N₂O₄] ÷ [NO₂]². 5) For 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic): increasing pressure shifts right; raising temperature shifts left; adding O₂ shifts right. 6) Equilibrium means equal rates, not equal amounts. 7) Why industry recycles unreacted gases — to convert more feedstock over repeated passes.

weeks.prep: Gather a plastic water bottle (not glass), a marker, a ruler, the freezer, sugar cubes, chalk (calcium carbonate sidewalk chalk works), water, vinegar, a baking pan, sand, a cup with a small hole for steady flow, and books to tilt the pan.
misconceptions: Students think ice is denser than water because solids usually are. Hydrogen bonds hold ice in an open hexagonal lattice, making it about 9% less dense than liquid water, so it floats and expands when freezing.
Students think dissolving means disappearing. The solute is still present, spread out as particles or ions among water molecules.
Students think erosion only happens in big floods. Slow, repeated processes (frost wedging, dissolution) shape landscapes over long times.

days.guide: Review hydrogen bonding. The student lists water's unique properties (high specific heat, ice less dense than liquid, high surface tension, excellent solvent, high heat of vaporization) and links each to hydrogen bonding and an Earth effect.

questions.q: Why does ice float?
questions.a: Hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, making ice less dense than liquid water.

questions.q: How does water's high specific heat affect Earth's climate?
questions.a: Oceans absorb and release large amounts of heat with little temperature change, moderating coastal climates.

days.guide: Fill a plastic bottle to the brim, cap it, mark dimensions, and freeze overnight. Measure the bulge, or fill a container to a line and measure the new height after freezing. Connect to frost wedging in rock cracks.

questions.q: If 500 mL of water freezes, about what volume of ice forms?
questions.a: About 545 mL (roughly 9% larger).

questions.q: Explain frost wedging.
questions.a: Water seeps into cracks, freezes and expands, pushing the crack wider; repeated freeze-thaw breaks rocks apart.

days.guide: Drop a sugar cube and a piece of chalk into water, and another of each into vinegar; time dissolving and observe bubbles.

questions.q: Why does chalk fizz and dissolve in vinegar but not much in water?
questions.a: Chalk is calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid: CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.q: How does this model chemical weathering?
questions.a: Rainwater containing dissolved CO₂ forms weak carbonic acid that slowly dissolves limestone, forming caves and sinkholes.

days.guide: Build a sand slope in a baking pan, then pour water at slow and fast rates from the same height. The student sketches channels, deltas and where sediment is deposited.

questions.q: Where did sand get deposited and why?
questions.a: Where the water slowed (at the bottom of the slope or on inside bends), because slower water has less energy to carry sediment.

questions.q: How did faster flow change erosion?
questions.a: It cut deeper, wider channels and carried more and larger particles.

days.guide: The student writes the investigation report. Score with the rubric and revise.

questions.q: Give one California example of water shaping the land.
questions.a: Examples: frost wedging of Sierra granite creating talus slopes; rivers carving canyons; waves eroding coastal cliffs; limestone caves such as those in the Sierra foothills.

weeks.assessment_key: Investigation report rubric (HS-ESS2-5): 4 = Includes all three investigations with data (bottle volume increase ≈ 9%; chalk fizzes and dissolves faster in vinegar than water while sugar dissolves faster in water; faster flow carries more and larger sediment, cutting deeper channels); explains each with water's properties (expansion on freezing due to hydrogen-bonded lattice → frost wedging; water as a polar solvent and weak acids from dissolved CO₂ → chemical weathering of limestone; water's cohesion/mass and flow energy → erosion and deposition); connects to a California example (Sierra granite frost wedging, limestone caves, coastal and river erosion). 3 = data plus partial explanations. 2 = data only. 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Gather table salt, the kitchen scale, measuring cups, a 1-cup (≈ 250 mL) container, cabbage indicator, 10 household solutions (lemon juice, vinegar, soda, coffee, milk, tap water, baking soda solution, soap solution, diluted ammonia cleaner — never mix ammonia with bleach), droppers, and clear cups. Open PhET 'pH Scale'.
misconceptions: Students think pH 6 is twice as acidic as pH 3. Each pH unit is a factor of 10: pH 3 has 1,000 times more H₃O⁺ than pH 6.
Students think molarity uses liters of water added. Molarity = moles of solute per liter of total solution.
Students think neutralization makes something disappear. Acid and base form water and a salt.

days.guide: Model M = mol ÷ L. The student makes 250 mL of a 0.50 M salt solution (7.31 g NaCl dissolved, then water added to 250 mL total) and solves concentration problems.

questions.q: How many grams of NaCl are needed for 250 mL of 0.50 M solution?
What is the molarity of 10.0 g of NaOH (40.00 g/mol) in 500 mL of solution?

days.guide: The student adds indicator to each household solution, records colors, and ranks them by pH using a cabbage color chart (red ~1–2, pink ~3–4, purple ~5–7, blue ~8, green ~9–11, yellow ~12+).

questions.q: Which household items are acids?
questions.a: Lemon juice, vinegar, soda, coffee (and slightly, milk).

questions.q: What color would you expect for ammonia cleaner?
questions.a: Green (strongly basic).

days.guide: In PhET pH Scale, the student tests items and relates [H₃O⁺] to pH using the logarithmic scale; record a table of pH vs. [H₃O⁺].

questions.q: A solution has [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻⁵ M. What is its pH, and is it acidic?
questions.a: pH 5; acidic.

questions.q: How does [H₃O⁺] change if you dilute an acid tenfold?
questions.a: It drops by a factor of 10, so the pH rises by 1.

days.guide: Measure 10.0 mL of vinegar into a cup with indicator. Add 0.50 M baking-soda solution (2.1 g NaHCO₃ in 50 mL solution) a milliliter at a time, swirling, until the color turns purple-blue and stays. Calculate vinegar's molarity from the volume used.

questions.q: It took 16.6 mL of 0.50 M NaHCO₃ to neutralize 10.0 mL of vinegar. What is the vinegar's molarity?
questions.a: 0.0166 L × 0.50 = 0.0083 mol NaHCO₃ = 0.0083 mol acetic acid (1:1); 0.0083 ÷ 0.0100 L = 0.83 M (about 5% acetic acid).

questions.q: Why add base slowly near the endpoint?
questions.a: To avoid overshooting the exact point where the acid is just neutralized.

days.guide: Give the quiz with a calculator; collect the pH chart and titration data.

questions.q: How many times more H₃O⁺ is in lemon juice (pH 2) than in milk (pH 6.5)?
questions.a: About 10^4.5 ≈ 32,000 times.

weeks.assessment_key: pH chart: full credit for 10 solutions ranked with color observations and approximate pH (lemon ~2, vinegar ~2.5–3, soda ~3, coffee ~5, milk ~6.5, water ~7, baking soda ~8–8.5, soap ~9–10, ammonia ~11–12). Titration data: volume of baking-soda solution needed to reach the endpoint (purple/blue color change) in a measured vinegar sample, with mole calculation (e.g., 10.0 mL of 0.83 M vinegar contains 0.0083 mol acetic acid; with 0.50 M NaHCO₃ the endpoint is about 16.6 mL). Quiz key: 1) Molarity of 0.50 mol NaCl in 2.0 L — 0.25 M. 2) Grams of NaCl for 250 mL of 0.50 M — 7.31 g. 3) pH when [H₃O⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M — 3. 4) How many times more acidic is pH 3 than pH 5 — 100. 5) Products of HCl + NaOH — NaCl + H₂O. 6) Acidic, basic or neutral: pH 9 — basic. 7) Moles of HCl in 25.0 mL of 0.100 M — 0.00250 mol.

weeks.prep: Gather cabbage indicator, a straw, eggshells (from about 4 eggs, rinsed and dried) or seashells, vinegar, water, two jars, and the kitchen scale. Bookmark NOAA's Hawaii Ocean Time-series (HOT) pH/pCO₂ graph (Station ALOHA) and readings on California oyster hatcheries and pteropods (NOAA Ocean Acidification Program). Build the Unit 8 test from the key.
misconceptions: Students think the ocean is becoming acidic (below pH 7). Seawater is still basic (~pH 8.05); 'acidification' means it is shifting toward acidic — a ~0.1 drop since preindustrial times, about a 26–30% increase in H⁺.
Students think acid directly dissolves all shells in the ocean now. The bigger problem is reduced carbonate ion availability, which makes building shells harder, especially for larvae and pteropods.
Students think vinegar is a realistic ocean model. It is far more acidic; it models the direction of the effect, not its speed.

days.guide: Put purple cabbage indicator water in a cup and have the student blow gently through a straw (never suck) for 1–3 minutes, watching for a color change. Write the equations.

questions.q: Why does the indicator turn pinker when you exhale into it?
questions.a: Exhaled CO₂ dissolves and forms carbonic acid (CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻), lowering the pH.

questions.q: How is this like the ocean?
questions.a: The ocean absorbs about a quarter of human CO₂ emissions, which forms carbonic acid and lowers seawater pH.

days.guide: Weigh equal masses of eggshell into a jar of vinegar and a jar of water. Each day for three days, remove, pat dry, weigh, and return. The student calculates percent mass change.

questions.q: Shells in vinegar went from 10.0 g to 6.5 g. What percent was lost?
Why is there a control jar of water?
questions.a: To show that the mass loss is caused by the acid, not by soaking or handling.

days.guide: Using the HOT/Station ALOHA graph, the student describes trends in seawater pCO₂ and pH since 1988 and calculates the approximate rate of pH change.

questions.q: What relationship do the HOT data show between ocean CO₂ and pH?
questions.a: As dissolved CO₂ rises (tracking atmospheric CO₂), pH falls — an inverse relationship.

questions.q: If pH fell from 8.11 to 8.05 over 30 years, what is the rate?
questions.a: 0.06 ÷ 30 = 0.002 pH units per year (0.02 per decade).

days.guide: The student researches effects on California and West Coast shellfish: oyster hatchery larvae failures in the late 2000s when corrosive upwelled water reached hatcheries, monitoring and buffering now used by hatcheries, and pteropod shell dissolution observed off the West Coast. Write a summary with sources.

questions.q: Why are oyster larvae especially vulnerable?
questions.a: They must build their first shells quickly, and low carbonate water makes that harder and more energy-costly.

questions.q: Why do pteropods matter to the food web?
questions.a: These tiny swimming snails are food for fish such as salmon, so their decline can ripple up the food chain.

days.guide: Give the Unit 8 test. Grade together and collect the shell lab.

questions.q: Write the equation showing how added H⁺ reduces carbonate ions in seawater.
questions.a: H⁺ + CO₃²⁻ → HCO₃⁻

weeks.assessment_key: Shell lab: full credit for daily mass table for shells in vinegar vs. water, percent mass lost (vinegar shells lose much more; water shells nearly constant), bubbles noted, equation CaCO₃ + 2CH₃COOH → Ca(CH₃COO)₂ + H₂O + CO₂, and a caveat about vinegar being far more acidic than seawater. Unit 8 test key (sample): 1) Water expands ~9% when it freezes because of its open hydrogen-bonded lattice. 2) Molarity of 1.5 mol in 3.0 L — 0.50 M. 3) pH 4 vs. pH 7: 1,000× more H₃O⁺. 4) CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. 5) Added H⁺ combines with CO₃²⁻ to make HCO₃⁻, lowering carbonate available for CaCO₃ shells. 6) Surface ocean pH dropped from about 8.2 to about 8.1 (now ~8.05). 7) Breathing into indicator turns it from purple toward pink (more acidic). 8) A buffer resists changes in pH. 9) Neutralization: HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. 10) Chalk dissolves faster in vinegar than water — acid reacts with carbonate.

weeks.prep: Help the student choose a challenge and gather supplies for the prototype (e.g., for a water filter: a cut plastic bottle, coffee filter, sand, gravel, activated charcoal from a pet store, muddy water — the filtered water is not safe to drink; for an insulated container: boxes, foam, foil, thermometer). Prepare the capstone rubric to share at the start.
misconceptions: Students start building before defining criteria. Require written criteria and constraints first so the test has something to measure.
Students cite only one website. Require three sources, including one government or peer-reviewed source.
Students treat a prototype failure as failure. A failed test produces data for redesign; that is engineering.

days.guide: Discuss three options. The student chooses one and writes a problem statement, at least three criteria (measurable) and two constraints.

questions.q: For an activated-charcoal water filter, give a measurable criterion.
questions.a: Example: reduces turbidity so text is readable through 10 cm of water, or removes a set amount of food dye color within 2 minutes.

questions.q: Give a constraint.
questions.a: Example: total materials cost under $10, or uses only household materials.

days.guide: The student finds three sources (at least one .gov, .edu or peer-reviewed) and writes notes on the chemistry of the problem and solution, with citations.

questions.q: How does activated charcoal remove contaminants?
questions.a: Adsorption: molecules stick to the charcoal's enormous internal surface area (hundreds of m² per gram).

questions.q: Why is source quality important?
questions.a: Reliable sources reduce the chance of basing the design on wrong information.

days.guide: The student builds and tests the prototype, recording quantitative data and at least two trials.

questions.q: Why run more than one trial?
questions.a: To check that results are repeatable and to estimate variability.

questions.q: Is filtered muddy water safe to drink?
questions.a: No — the filter does not reliably remove bacteria or viruses; it must be disinfected or boiled.

days.guide: The student evaluates the prototype against each criterion in a table (met / partly / not met) and lists trade-offs and improvements.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'evaluating' and 'describing' a design?
questions.a: Evaluating judges performance against criteria using data; describing only tells what was built.

days.guide: The student drafts a slide presentation (8–10 slides). Review with the rubric and give two specific suggestions.

questions.q: What should the data slide include?
questions.a: A graph or table with labeled units and a one-sentence takeaway.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone checkpoint rubric (4 levels): 4 = Problem statement; at least three measurable criteria and two constraints; chemistry explained with three cited sources (e.g., adsorption of contaminants onto activated carbon's huge surface area; insulation reducing conduction/convection/radiation); prototype built and tested with quantitative data (e.g., turbidity rating before/after, temperature drop over time); evaluation against each criterion with trade-offs; draft slides with title, problem, chemistry, design, data, evaluation, next steps. 3 = all parts present but data or chemistry thin. 2 = missing testing or sources. 1 = idea only.

weeks.prep: Arrange the capstone presentation with family. Build a cumulative final exam from the key (about 40 items, 90 minutes, periodic table and formula sheet allowed). Have the Week 1 candle questions and the driving-question board ready.
misconceptions: Students memorize answers to past quizzes rather than practicing new problems. Use fresh numbers in review.
Students skip units on the final. Deduct for missing units on calculations.
Students write the final candle explanation as a list. It should be a connected explanation linking atoms, bonds, energy and the Earth system.

days.guide: The student presents the capstone (10 minutes) and answers questions. Score with the capstone rubric and share one strength and one improvement.

questions.q: Ask: What would you change if you had another month?
questions.a: A strong answer names a specific weakness shown by the data and a concrete redesign.

days.guide: Mixed review covering all units: equations, stoichiometry, energy, bonding, equilibrium, pH, climate. Reteach anything missed.

questions.q: How many grams of CO₂ form from 0.10 mol of NaHCO₃ reacting with excess vinegar?
A reaction is endothermic. On an energy diagram, are the products higher or lower than the reactants?
questions.a: Higher.

days.guide: Give the final exam in one 90-minute sitting.

questions.q: (After the exam) Which unit felt strongest and which weakest?
questions.a: Answers vary; use them to guide Day 4 corrections.

days.guide: Return the exam. The student corrects every missed item and writes the reason for each error (concept, careless, units).

questions.q: Why categorize errors?
questions.a: It shows whether mistakes come from misunderstanding or carelessness, guiding what to practice.

days.guide: The student writes a final, connected explanation of the burning candle using ideas from every unit and compares it to the Week 1 questions.

questions.q: In one sentence, where does the candle's mass go and where does its energy come from?
questions.a: The wax's carbon and hydrogen atoms combine with oxygen to form CO₂ and H₂O gases that enter the air (conserving mass), and the energy comes from forming stronger bonds in those products than were broken in the wax and oxygen.

weeks.assessment_key: Capstone rubric: 4 = clear problem and criteria, accurate chemistry, data-driven evaluation, trade-offs, confident delivery, answers questions. Final exam key (sample core items): 1) Balance C₃H₈ + O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O with 5O₂. 2) 200 g water warmed 15 °C absorbs 12,550 J. 3) Neutrons in ¹⁴C — 8. 4) 40 g of an isotope with half-life 10 yr after 30 yr — 5 g. 5) Ionic formula of calcium chloride — CaCl₂. 6) Shape of CO₂ — linear, nonpolar. 7) Moles in 88 g CO₂ — 2.0. 8) Grams CO₂ from 8.4 g NaHCO₃ (0.10 mol) — 4.4 g. 9) Limiting reactant: 3.0 mol H₂ and 1.0 mol O₂ → O₂ limits, 2.0 mol H₂O. 10) ΔH for CH₄ combustion from bond energies — −802 kJ/mol. 11) Exothermic reaction, temperature raised — shifts left. 12) pH 3 vs. pH 6 — 1,000× more acidic. 13) Why CO₂ is a greenhouse gas — absorbs infrared. 14) Ocean acidification reduces carbonate ions. 15) Positive feedback example — ice-albedo. Final candle explanation rubric: 4 = connects wax hydrocarbon structure, combustion equation and conservation of mass, bond energies explaining the release of energy, CO₂'s role in the greenhouse effect and the carbon cycle, and ocean uptake.
